questions.q: According to the Singer and Nicolson fluid mosaic model, how are biological membranes structurally organized?
options: Fluid phospholipid bilayer with amphipathic proteins embedded in or on it
A rigid trilaminar protein-lipid-protein sandwich with fixed pores
A monolayer of triglycerides coated by cholesterol esters
questions.explain: The fluid mosaic model describes membranes as a two-dimensional fluid lipid bilayer in which integral and peripheral membrane proteins diffuse laterally.

open.q: Name the model proposed by Singer and Nicolson to describe the dynamic structure of biological membranes.

questions.q: Which property of phospholipids drives their spontaneous self-assembly into bilayers in an aqueous environment?
options: Covalent crosslinks between fatty acyl tails
Amphipathic: polar heads and hydrophobic fatty acyl tails
Net positive charge on all head groups
High solubility of fatty acyl chains in water
questions.explain: Amphipathic phospholipids bury their hydrophobic hydrocarbon tails away from water via the hydrophobic effect while exposing polar head groups to the aqueous phase.

open.q: What chemical term describes molecules like phospholipids that contain both hydrophilic and hydrophobic regions?

questions.q: Which is the most abundant glycerophospholipid in eukaryotic plasma membranes?
questions.explain: Phosphatidylcholine (lecithin) is the predominant structural phospholipid of eukaryotic cell membranes, concentrated largely in the outer leaflet.

open.q: Name the most abundant phospholipid in eukaryotic cell membranes.

questions.q: How does cholesterol modulate the fluidity of eukaryotic plasma membranes across varying temperatures?
options: Increases fluidity at high temperatures and decreases fluidity at low temperatures
Eliminates all lateral diffusion of membrane proteins
Forms covalent ester bonds with sphingomyelin
Restrains acyl chains when warm and prevents tight packing when cold
questions.explain: Cholesterol acts as a bidirectional fluidity buffer: its rigid steroid ring restricts fatty acyl chain movement at warm temperatures while disrupting ordered crystalline packing of saturated chains at cold temperatures.

open.q: Which sterol acts as a bidirectional buffer of membrane fluidity in eukaryotic plasma membranes?

questions.q: How do cis double bonds in unsaturated fatty acyl chains affect membrane fluidity and transition temperature (Tm)?
options: Kinks prevent tight packing, raising fluidity and lowering Tm
Allow tighter van der Waals packing, decreasing fluidity and raising Tm
Eliminate the hydrophobic core of the bilayer
questions.explain: Cis double bonds create ~30-degree bends in hydrocarbon tails, reducing van der Waals interactions between neighboring chains, increasing fluidity, and lowering the melting transition temperature.

open.q: Do cis-unsaturated fatty acyl chains increase or decrease the melting transition temperature (Tm) of a lipid bilayer?

questions.q: Which two choline-containing lipid classes are enriched predominantly in the outer (exoplasmic) leaflet of the mammalian plasma membrane?
questions.explain: The outer leaflet is enriched in phosphatidylcholine, sphingomyelin, and glycosphingolipids, whereas the inner cytosolic leaflet is enriched in phosphatidylethanolamine, phosphatidylserine, and phosphatidylinositol.

open.q: Name the two major choline-containing phospholipids concentrated in the outer leaflet of the plasma membrane.

questions.q: Externalization of which inner-leaflet aminophospholipid to the outer plasma membrane surface serves as an 'eat-me' signal for macrophage phagocytosis during apoptosis and promotes coagulation on activated platelets?
questions.explain: Phosphatidylserine carries a net negative charge and is normally restricted to the inner leaflet by flippases; scramblase-mediated exposure on the outer leaflet triggers apoptotic clearance and provides a docking surface for clotting factor complexes.

open.q: Name the negatively charged inner-leaflet phospholipid whose exposure on the outer membrane signals apoptosis and supports blood coagulation.

questions.q: Which class of ATP-dependent P4-ATPase enzymes maintains membrane lipid asymmetry by actively transporting phosphatidylserine and phosphatidylethanolamine from the outer leaflet to the inner cytosolic leaflet?
questions.explain: Flippases (P4-ATPases) use ATP to move aminophospholipids inward to the cytosolic leaflet, floppases (ABC transporters) move lipids outward, and Ca2+-activated scramblases randomize lipids bidirectionally without ATP.

open.q: Name the ATP-dependent enzymes that translocate phospholipids from the outer leaflet to the inner cytosolic leaflet.

questions.q: What are lipid rafts in eukaryotic plasma membranes?
options: Cholesterol- and sphingolipid-rich ordered signaling microdomains
Areas devoid of cholesterol composed purely of short-chain fatty acids
questions.explain: Lipid rafts are detergent-resistant, liquid-ordered membrane microdomains densely packed with cholesterol and saturated sphingolipids that organize signal transduction complexes and caveolae.

open.q: Which two lipid classes are specifically enriched inside plasma membrane lipid rafts?

questions.q: Which type of membrane movement occurs rapidly and spontaneously within a single leaflet of a lipid bilayer without enzymatic catalysis?
questions.explain: Phospholipids diffuse laterally within the same leaflet at ~10^-8 cm2/s, whereas transverse flip-flop across the hydrophobic core is extremely slow unless catalyzed by flippases, floppases, or scramblases.

open.q: Which type of phospholipid diffusion (lateral or transverse flip-flop) occurs rapidly without enzymatic assistance in a lipid bilayer?

questions.q: Which laboratory reagents are required to extract integral (intrinsic) transmembrane proteins from a biological membrane?
options: High-salt buffers or EDTA chelating agents
Detergents or organic solvents that disrupt the bilayer
questions.explain: Integral membrane proteins span or embed deeply into the hydrophobic core and require amphipathic detergents (e.g., SDS, Triton X-100) to solubilize them, whereas peripheral proteins detach with high salt or pH changes.

open.q: What class of amphipathic reagents is required to solubilize integral transmembrane proteins from the lipid bilayer?

questions.q: Which secondary protein structure most commonly spans the hydrophobic core of mammalian plasma membranes in single-pass and multipass transmembrane proteins?
questions.explain: An alpha-helix of ~20-25 hydrophobic amino acids (~3.6 residues per turn, 0.15 nm rise per residue) spans the ~3.0-3.5 nm hydrocarbon core while satisfying all backbone hydrogen bonds internally.

open.q: Name the predominant secondary structure formed by membrane-spanning segments of eukaryotic transmembrane proteins.

questions.q: Which secondary structural motif forms large water-filled transmembrane channels (porins) in the outer membranes of Gram-negative bacteria, mitochondria, and chloroplasts?
questions.explain: Antiparallel amphipathic beta-strands roll into a transmembrane beta-barrel with hydrophobic side chains facing the lipid bilayer and hydrophilic residues lining the aqueous pore.

open.q: Name the beta-sheet tertiary motif that forms porin channels in outer mitochondrial and Gram-negative bacterial membranes.

questions.q: Which lipid anchor attaches certain extracellular surface proteins (such as alkaline phosphatase, decay-accelerating factor CD55, and acetylcholinesterase) exclusively to the outer leaflet of the plasma membrane?
questions.explain: GPI anchors link the C-terminus of proteins via phosphoethanolamine and an oligosaccharide core to phosphatidylinositol in the outer leaflet; defective GPI anchor synthesis (PIGA mutation) causes paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria.

open.q: Name the glycolipid anchor that tethers proteins such as CD55 and CD59 to the outer surface of the plasma membrane.

questions.q: A 24-year-old man presents with recurrent hemolytic anemia, splenomegaly, jaundice, and pigmented gallstones. Peripheral blood smear shows spherocytes lacking central pallor, and osmotic fragility is increased. Which erythrocyte membrane cytoskeletal protein is most commonly defective?
questions.explain: Hereditary spherocytosis is caused by mutations in vertical red cell membrane skeleton proteins (ankyrin, spectrin, Band 3, or protein 4.2), causing membrane microvesicle loss, reduced surface-to-volume ratio, and splenic trapping.

open.q: Name the primary meshwork protein of the erythrocyte membrane skeleton whose defect causes hereditary spherocytosis and elliptocytosis.

questions.q: Where is the glycocalyx located on mammalian cells, and what is its primary biochemical composition?
options: Inner leaflet; actin and tubulin meshwork
Extracellular surface; carbohydrate chains of glycoproteins
questions.explain: Oligosaccharides on membrane glycoproteins and glycolipids always face the extracellular space (or organelle lumen), forming the negatively charged glycocalyx involved in cell recognition, adhesion, and protection.

open.q: On which side of the plasma membrane (extracellular or cytosolic) are the carbohydrate chains of glycoproteins and glycolipids exclusively oriented?

questions.q: How does facilitated diffusion differ kinetically from simple diffusion across a lipid bilayer?
options: It shows saturation kinetics (Vmax, Km) and stereospecificity, unlike simple diffusion
Facilitated diffusion requires direct ATP hydrolysis
Simple diffusion requires transmembrane carrier proteins
Facilitated diffusion moves solutes against their electrochemical gradient
questions.explain: Facilitated diffusion uses specific carrier or channel proteins, so transport rate plateaus (Vmax) when all binding sites are saturated, while remaining passive down the electrochemical gradient.

open.q: What kinetic property distinguishes carrier-mediated facilitated diffusion from simple diffusion at high substrate concentrations?

questions.q: Which class of solutes crosses a pure phospholipid bilayer most rapidly by simple diffusion without a transport protein?
options: Large polar uncharged molecules like glucose
Small nonpolar hydrophobic molecules like O2, CO2, and N2
Monovalent cations like Na+ and K+
questions.explain: Small hydrophobic gases (O2, CO2, N2) and lipophilic molecules (steroid hormones, ethanol) partition readily into the nonpolar hydrocarbon core, whereas ions are excluded by their hydration shells.

open.q: Give two examples of small nonpolar molecules that diffuse rapidly across pure lipid bilayers without transporters.

questions.q: How do potassium (K+) channels achieve high selectivity for K+ ions over smaller Na+ ions?
options: The channel pore is physically narrower than a dehydrated Na+ ion
Carbonyl oxygens in the filter mimic K+'s hydration shell
K+ ions bind covalently to ATP inside the pore
questions.explain: In the KcsA-type selectivity filter, carbonyl oxygen atoms are spaced at the exact distance to coordinate dehydrated K+ ions energetically, making dehydration of smaller Na+ ions thermodynamically unfavorable.

open.q: Which functional groups in the selectivity filter of potassium channels coordinate dehydrated K+ ions to achieve ion selectivity?

questions.q: Which family of tetrameric transmembrane water channels permits rapid osmotic water movement across cell membranes while excluding protons (H3O+)?
questions.explain: Aquaporins contain conserved NPA (Asn-Pro-Ala) motifs and an electrostatic arginine/histidine filter that orient water molecules to prevent proton hopping along a water wire.

open.q: Name the family of transmembrane channel proteins that facilitate rapid water transport across biological membranes without conducting protons.

questions.q: How does valinomycin act as a mobile carrier ionophore to dissipate mitochondrial membrane potentials?
options: Encapsulates K+ in a hydrophobic ring and carries it across the membrane
Moves protons through a beta-barrel channel
questions.explain: Valinomycin is a cyclic depsipeptide antibiotic with a hydrophobic exterior and oxygen-lined interior that selectively encapsulates K+ and diffuses across membranes as a mobile ion carrier.

open.q: Which specific cation is selectively transported across membranes by the mobile carrier ionophore valinomycin?

questions.q: Which erythrocyte anion exchanger mediates the electroneutral one-for-one exchange of bicarbonate (HCO3-) and chloride (Cl-) across the red blood cell membrane (the chloride shift)?
questions.explain: Band 3 (anion exchanger 1, AE1) is the most abundant integral membrane protein of human erythrocytes, catalyzing rapid 1:1 exchange of HCO3- and Cl- to boost venous CO2 carrying capacity.

open.q: Name the abundant erythrocyte integral membrane protein that mediates the chloride-bicarbonate shift.

questions.q: What is the exact transport stoichiometry of the plasma membrane Na+/K+-ATPase per molecule of ATP hydrolyzed?
options: 2 Na+ pumped out and 3 K+ pumped in
3 Na+ pumped in and 2 K+ pumped out
3 Na+ pumped out and 2 K+ pumped in
1 Na+ pumped out and 1 K+ pumped in
questions.explain: Na+/K+-ATPase is an electrogenic P-type ATPase that exports 3 Na+ ions out of the cell and imports 2 K+ ions into the cell per ATP hydrolyzed, contributing directly to the negative resting membrane potential.

open.q: State the number and direction of Na+ and K+ ions transported by Na+/K+-ATPase per ATP hydrolyzed.

questions.q: Which specific subunit and conformational state of Na+/K+-ATPase is bound and inhibited by cardiac glycosides such as digoxin and ouabain?
options: Intracellular beta subunit in the E1 state
Extracellular alpha subunit in the phosphorylated E2-P state
C-terminal tail of the gamma subunit
Catalytic ATP-binding pocket on the cytosolic side
questions.explain: Cardiac glycosides bind the extracellular surface of the catalytic alpha subunit in its phosphorylated E2-P conformation, blocking K+-stimulated dephosphorylation and raising intracellular Na+, which reduces Na+/Ca2+ exchanger activity and increases cardiac contractility.

open.q: Name the P-type ATPase pump inhibited by cardiac glycosides such as digoxin and ouabain.

questions.q: Which class of proton-pumping ATPases acidifies intracellular organelles such as lysosomes, endosomes, and synaptic vesicles without forming a phosphorylated enzyme intermediate?
questions.explain: V-type (vacuolar) H+-ATPases use ATP hydrolysis to pump protons into lysosomes, endosomes, osteoclast resorption lacunae, and renal intercalated cell lumens.

open.q: Name the class of proton pumps responsible for acidifying lysosomes and endosomes.

questions.q: How does secondary active transport (such as intestinal and renal SGLT1 glucose uptake) drive uphill solute accumulation against its concentration gradient?
options: Directly hydrolyzes ATP at the SGLT1 binding site
Couples uphill glucose uptake to the downhill Na+ gradient
Uses light energy to isomerize retinal
questions.explain: Secondary active symporters like SGLT1 harness the steep inward Na+ electrochemical gradient maintained by primary active Na+/K+-ATPase to cotransport Na+ and glucose into epithelial cells.

open.q: Name the apical Na+/glucose cotransporter responsible for secondary active glucose absorption in the small intestine.

questions.q: What is the physiological rationale for including both glucose and sodium in oral rehydration therapy (ORT) for acute secretory diarrhea such as cholera?
options: Glucose directly kills Vibrio cholerae bacteria
SGLT1 Na+-glucose cotransport survives cholera and drives water uptake
Sodium activates pepsinogen in the colon
questions.explain: Cholera toxin stimulates CFTR Cl- secretion and inhibits electroneutral NaCl absorption, but apical SGLT1 symporters remain functional, enabling coupled Na+, glucose, and osmotic water uptake.

open.q: Which intestinal cotransporter remains functional during cholera diarrhea and forms the physiological basis of oral rehydration therapy?

questions.q: A 6-year-old boy presents with recurrent Pseudomonas pulmonary infections, pancreatic insufficiency, and elevated sweat chloride (>60 mmol/L). The defective CFTR protein belongs to which superfamily of membrane transporters, even though it functions as a cAMP-regulated chloride channel?
questions.explain: CFTR (ABCC7) is a member of the ATP-binding cassette (ABC) superfamily that uses ATP binding/hydrolysis and PKA phosphorylation to gate an epithelial chloride channel; the most common mutation is Delta-F508 causing misfolding and ER degradation.

open.q: Name the chloride channel defective in cystic fibrosis that belongs to the ABC transporter superfamily.

questions.q: How does P-glycoprotein (MDR1 / ABCB1) confer multidrug resistance to cancer cells?
options: ATP-driven efflux pump for hydrophobic drugs
questions.explain: P-glycoprotein (ABCB1) is an ATP-binding cassette efflux pump that uses ATP hydrolysis to expel amphipathic chemotherapeutic agents (such as doxorubicin, vincristine, and paclitaxel) across the plasma membrane.

open.q: Name the ABC efflux transporter encoded by the MDR1 gene that pumps chemotherapeutic drugs out of tumor cells.

questions.q: Which coat protein complex forms a triskelion lattice to mediate receptor-mediated endocytosis (such as LDL uptake) from the plasma membrane and budding from the trans-Golgi network?
questions.explain: Clathrin heavy and light chains assemble into three-legged triskelions that polymerize into polyhedral cages around adaptor-selected cargo receptors during endocytosis.

open.q: Name the triskelion-forming coat protein required for receptor-mediated endocytosis of LDL particles.

questions.q: Which GTPase enzyme wraps around the neck of budding clathrin-coated pits and hydrolyzes GTP to pinch off the vesicle from the plasma membrane?
questions.explain: Dynamin is a large mechanochemical GTPase that polymerizes into a helical collar around the neck of invaginated clathrin-coated pits and constricts upon GTP hydrolysis to sever the vesicle.

open.q: Name the GTPase that constricts and severs budding clathrin-coated vesicles from the plasma membrane.

questions.q: Which vesicular coat protein complex mediates anterograde transport from the rough endoplasmic reticulum to the Golgi apparatus, and which mediates retrograde transport from the Golgi back to the ER?
options: COPI mediates anterograde ER-to-Golgi; COPII mediates retrograde Golgi-to-ER
COPII anterograde ER-to-Golgi; COPI retrograde Golgi-to-ER
Clathrin mediates both ER-to-Golgi and Golgi-to-ER
Caveolin mediates ER-to-Golgi; spectrin mediates Golgi-to-ER
questions.explain: COPII-coated vesicles carry newly synthesized secretory proteins forward (anterograde) from ER exit sites to the cis-Golgi, while COPI-coated vesicles retrieve KDEL-tagged ER resident proteins backward (retrograde).

open.q: Which coat protein complex mediates anterograde vesicle transport from the endoplasmic reticulum to the Golgi apparatus?

questions.q: How do SNARE proteins drive specific membrane fusion during exocytosis and intracellular vesicle trafficking?
options: v-SNAREs and t-SNAREs form a bundle that draws membranes together
questions.explain: Pairing of cognate v-SNAREs and t-SNAREs forms a tight trans-SNARE four-helix coiled-coil bundle that overcomes the repulsive hydration barrier between membranes to drive bilayer fusion; NSF and alpha-SNAP use ATP to dissociate SNAREs afterward.

open.q: Name the family of complementary vesicle and target membrane proteins that form a four-helix bundle to drive membrane fusion.

questions.q: Which specialized intercellular junctions form a continuous paracellular seal near the apical border of epithelial cells, preventing solute leakage between cells and maintaining apical-basolateral membrane polarity?
questions.explain: Tight junctions composed of claudins and occludins seal the paracellular space and act as a 'fence' preventing apical and basolateral membrane proteins/lipids from mixing.

open.q: Name the apical epithelial cell junctions formed by claudins and occludins that seal the paracellular pathway and maintain membrane polarity.

questions.q: Which intercellular junctions consist of paired hexameric connexon hemichannels that allow direct electrical and metabolic coupling of ions and small molecules (<1,000 Da) between adjacent cells?
questions.explain: Gap junctions are formed by two aligned connexons (each built from six connexin subunits), permitting rapid spread of action potentials in cardiac and smooth muscle and metabolic cooperation between cells.

open.q: Name the protein subunits that oligomerize into hexameric connexons to form gap junctions.

questions.q: Which calcium-dependent transmembrane cell-adhesion proteins link the intracellular keratin intermediate filaments of adjacent epithelial cells at desmosomes (maculae adherentes)?
questions.explain: Desmosomal cadherins (desmogleins and desmocollins) mediate Ca2+-dependent homophilic adhesion between cells and anchor via plakoglobin/desmoplakin to intermediate filaments; autoantibodies against desmoglein-3 cause pemphigus vulgaris.

open.q: Name the calcium-dependent cell-adhesion protein family found at adherens junctions and desmosomes.

questions.q: Why does the inner mitochondrial membrane have an unusually high protein-to-lipid ratio (~75-80% protein by weight) and contain cardiolipin while lacking cholesterol?
options: Contains respiratory complexes and translocases; its inner membrane limits proton leak
questions.explain: The inner mitochondrial membrane is the site of oxidative phosphorylation and metabolite transport, requiring massive concentrations of respiratory proteins and cardiolipin to prevent proton leaks.

open.q: Which cellular membrane has the highest protein-to-lipid ratio (~75-80% protein) in eukaryotic cells?

questions.q: In contrast to the inner mitochondrial membrane, why does the myelin sheath of Schwann cells and oligodendrocytes have an exceptionally high lipid-to-protein ratio (~80% lipid)?
options: Its lipid layers insulate axons and enable saltatory conduction
questions.explain: Myelin acts as an electrical insulator around axons; its ~80% lipid composition minimizes transmembrane ion leakage and accelerates action potential propagation between nodes of Ranvier.

open.q: Which specialized nervous system membrane structure contains approximately 80% lipid and 20% protein to provide electrical insulation?

questions.q: How is the membrane-spanning domain of a single-pass transmembrane protein identified from its primary amino acid sequence using a hydropathy plot?
options: A hydrophobic stretch of about 20–25 amino acids
A run of arginine and lysine residues
questions.explain: Hydropathy plots (such as Kyte-Doolittle) score each residue's free energy of transfer from water to a nonpolar solvent; a peak of ~20 consecutive hydrophobic residues predicts a transmembrane alpha-helix.

open.q: What analytical plot graphs amino acid hydrophobicity along a polypeptide sequence to predict transmembrane segments?

questions.q: What is the biochemical basis of the resting membrane potential (~-70 mV) across a typical mammalian plasma membrane?
options: Equal permeability of the resting membrane to Na+ and K+
High K+ leak conductance pulls the membrane toward E_K
Inward diffusion of negatively charged plasma albumin
Active inward pumping of chloride ions by ATP synthase
questions.explain: Na+/K+-ATPase maintains high intracellular K+ and low intracellular Na+, while resting plasma membranes are far more permeable to K+ than Na+ via K+ leak channels, driving the membrane potential close to the K+ equilibrium potential.

open.q: To which specific ion is a resting mammalian cell plasma membrane most permeable?

questions.q: How does omeprazole (a proton pump inhibitor) suppress gastric acid secretion at the parietal cell apical membrane?
options: Inhibits carbonic anhydrase inside parietal cells
Covalently inactivates the P-type H+/K+-ATPase proton pump
Neutralizes secreted HCl directly in the stomach lumen
questions.explain: Omeprazole is an acid-activated prodrug that concentrates in parietal cell secretory canaliculi and covalently inhibits cysteine residues on the luminal side of the P-type H+/K+-ATPase.

open.q: Name the P-type ATPase pump on gastric parietal cells irreversibly inhibited by omeprazole.

questions.q: Which antiport exchanger in cardiac myocyte plasma membranes uses the inward Na+ gradient to extrude cytosolic Ca2+ during diastole?
questions.explain: The Na+/Ca2+ exchanger (NCX) imports 3 Na+ ions down their electrochemical gradient to export 1 Ca2+ ion; digoxin raises intracellular Na+, reducing NCX Ca2+ extrusion and increasing sarcoplasmic reticulum Ca2+ stores.

open.q: Name the plasma membrane antiporter in cardiomyocytes that exchanges 3 Na+ ions for 1 Ca2+ ion to extrude calcium.

questions.q: A 31-year-old woman with familial hypercholesterolemia has normal LDL receptor synthesis and surface binding, yet LDL particles fail to internalize into hepatocytes. Mutation in which cytoplasmic tail motif of the LDL receptor prevents clustering into clathrin-coated pits?
questions.explain: The cytoplasmic tail of the LDL receptor contains an NPXY (Asn-Pro-X-Tyr) sorting signal recognized by AP2/ARH adaptor proteins to recruit the receptor into clathrin-coated pits.

open.q: Name the four-residue C-terminal tetrapeptide sequence that retains soluble ER-resident proteins by triggering retrograde COPI retrieval from the Golgi.

questions.q: How do hemidesmosomes differ structurally and functionally from desmosomes?
options: Hemidesmosomes use cadherins to link adjacent cells, whereas desmosomes use integrins
Hemidesmosomes use integrins to anchor keratin to the basement membrane; desmosomes join cells via cadherins
Hemidesmosomes connect actin microfilaments, whereas desmosomes connect microtubules
Hemidesmosomes allow ion passage between cells, whereas desmosomes block diffusion
questions.explain: Hemidesmosomes link intracellular keratin intermediate filaments to basement membrane laminin via integrins and plectin (targeted in bullous pemphigoid), whereas desmosomes join adjacent cells via cadherins.

open.q: Name the transmembrane heterodimeric adhesion receptors that anchor cells to extracellular matrix proteins such as fibronectin and laminin.

questions.q: What happens to red blood cells placed in a hypotonic saline solution (e.g., 0.3% NaCl)?
options: Water leaves the cells, causing crenation
Water enters osmotically, causing swelling and hemolysis
questions.explain: Because the plasma membrane is freely permeable to water via aquaporin-1 but impermeable to solutes, extracellular hypotonicity drives osmotic water influx until the erythrocyte swells and lyses.

open.q: What term describes the shrinking and spiked appearance of red blood cells placed in a hypertonic solution?
